The Good Messenger: mRNA's Promise for More Effective Medicine

By: John Webb | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We examine how the mRNA technology behind several of the COVID vaccines could unlock new ways of fighting other diseases.

Unique Selling Point:
Thanks to the extraordinary efforts of leading scientists, the world has been exposed to the wonders of Messenger RNA and its ability to ward off severe COVID19 and, possibly, infection with SARSCoV2. Many, though, are unaware of exactly what mRNA is and how the technology works. We aim to answer those questions while revealing how the success in developing mRNA-based vaccines might lead to new, more effective treatments for other viruses and diseases. It's a case of a unique technology, perfected in unique times, leading to unprecedented advances in modern medicine.

Summary:
Imagine a species so advanced it’s able to replicate the functioning of the human body at a molecular level, one with the audacity to grow in a lab a crucial element of how human cells function and then inject them into actual, living beings. Well, thanks to breakthroughs in Genome sequencing and advances in other areas of medicine, that is precisely what our species is now able to do. It’s a technology at the cutting edge of science and crucial to our attempts to defeat the SARS-CoV-2 virus. However, this is not a Covid story.
mRNA is a molecule containing the instructions by which cells make proteins - essential to how our bodies function. What’s the point of proteins? Well, in scientific terms they “are large, complex molecules that play many critical roles in the body. They do most of the work in cells and are required for the structure, function, and regulation of the body’s tissues and organs.” In other words, they’re very important not only to the healthy functioning of our biological systems but to the development of disease and – hopefully – our body’s ability to deal with it.

The use of mRNA as the foundational technology in the development of two of the current generation of Covid vaccines (by which our body is “tricked” into making antibodies by recognising a section of the virus’s now infamous spike protein) has confirmed what many have believed for several decades: it's a natural biological process that can be manipulated to help our bodies fight other viruses and diseases. In the southern African context, HIV is one that often comes to mind.

So, how does the technology work in lay terms? How did we stumble upon it? Could the darkness of this global pandemic thrust us into the light of a new and infinitely more successful way of treating those suffering currently incurable diseases? And how close might we be to a HIV vaccine, for example?


Further information:
While the development of mRNA-based vaccines has been nothing short of miraculous, those in the know highlight that SARS-CoV-2 is a simpler target than what is presented by other viruses - notably HIV. That's not to say the technology doesn't offer a potentially game-changing approach to how they're treated, merely that much research and study lies ahead to fully unlock its potential.

Script:


VO: The coffee shop is still quieter than you’d expect, the face mask still close to hand but 12 months since COVID19 was declared a pandemic, things feel a little different. (PAUSE) After so much uncertainty and loss there’s a glimmer of hope: vaccines.

Link: the past year has been tough: Many have died, others are battling the side effects of infection. Those lucky enough avoid catching it, are dealing with the psychological impact of lockdown and social distancing. But, what if, when we look back on this period in our history, we’ll see it as the moment modern medicine underwent a revolution?

VO: Among the vaccines being rolled out globally, two have attracted significant attention – and not only because of their impact on COVID19. (PAUSE) Developed by Moderna and a collaboration between Pfizer and Biontech, they rely on something called Messenger RNA, or mRNA. It’s a molecule that could dramatically change how we treat other viruses and diseases, too.

Upsound Saidy Brown [07:06 – 07:12] *Clears throat* How do you deal with stress? *sips water*

VO: Meet 25-year-old Saidy Brown. As a person living with a chronic disease during a pandemic, she can be forgiven her moments of stress…

Upsound Saidy Brown [07:12 – 07:13] *Finishes water* No, MmMmm.

VO: … yet she’s determined to continue educating people about the virus and spends much of her time answering questions and sharing her thoughts online.
(PAUSE)

VO: We’ve asked Saidy for an interview because her story helps to tell another: how mRNA vaccine technology might just change the lives of future Saidy Browns.
(PAUSE)

VO: Saidy was born with HIV but she was only diagnosed at 14. At 18 she went on life-saving anti-retroviral drugs.
ITV Saidy Brown [14:54:19:14 - 14:54:50:19] I was quite confused. I genuinely thought there was a mistake because I remember the first thing I said was, “but I'm just 14. I didn't do anything”

VO: After a period of denial, she accepted her status and grew into the role of HIV advocate – what she calls HI-Victor.
(PAUSE)

VO: And yet you can’t escape the inevitable sorrow in Saidy’s story.

ITV Saidy Brown [15:13:20:23 - 15:13:51:20] STRAP “HIV Advocate” in as much as I am so vocal about my HIV status, I am a human being, too. (CUT) Had there been a cure for HIV, I would not even be here sitting with you speaking about HIV, because it would have just been that illness that I contracted and was cured of. (CUT) the journey of living with HIV is not as easy sometimes as we make it out to be.

VO: HIV is treatable, and even preventable thanks to a daily pill known as pre-exposure prophylaxis. But it remains incurable and there’s no vaccine.

VO: I’ve come to the Antiviral Gene Therapy Research Unit at WITS University to find out why and how that might one day no longer be the case – not only for HIV, but other viruses and diseases.
(PAUSE)

VO: Professor Patrick Arbuthnot heads up a crack team researching how genes can be utilised to treat or prevent viral diseases like Hepatitis B - a virus that attacks the liver. Like many in their field, they’ve also turned their attention to COVID19. We’ve asked the Professor to help demystify the technology behind mRNA vaccines.

ITV Patrick Arbuthnot [10:52:27:22 - 10:53:10:11] what happens normally in a cell - in your cells or my cells - is that the DNA, which is our genetic makeup, sends a message through the messenger RNA and that's what's called a messenger RNA. And that messenger RNA then gets translated into a protein.

VO: It’s complex science, but where there’s a lab, there’s usually a whiteboard.
(PAUSE)

VO: That’s the SARS-CoV-2 virus with its infamous thorns or spike proteins. Like the Professor said, mRNA molecules contain genetic instructions for making proteins – think of them as a kind of instruction booklet. These proteins are vital for the body to function properly. (PAUSE) mRNA vaccines deliver synthetic or artificial mRNA into cells, instructing them to make only the spike part of the virus. The immune system identifies them as foreign invaders and kicks into gear. If a vaccinated person is later exposed to SARS-CoV-2, the immune system now recognises the spikes and produces antibodies to try and neutralise them. (PAUSE) So, it’s genetic technology that mimics a natural biological process inside our cells and – because of the COVID pandemic - we now have proof it works.

ITV Professor Arbuthnot [10:55:41:21 - 10:55:52:18]STRAP “Director: WITS/SAMRC, Antiviral Gene Therapy Research Unit” It's a field that's been developing over several years, I think it's more than 20 years that people have been working on trying to develop mRNA as a therapeutic or as a vaccine (CUT) [10:55:54:14 - 10:56:26:11] it's really been sorting out the technology that accompanies the efficient production of the mRNA to enable it to work as a vaccine or a therapeutic.

VO: Among many techniques yet to be perfected is how best to get the mRNA into the cells – quite literary, how to deliver the message.

ITV Professor Arbuthnot [10:57:04:13 - 10:57:34:19] They have to be put into a little capsule, a little delivery mechanism to get into the target cell. And very often what's used are also called lipid nanoparticles, that tiny little lipid droplets that incorporate the mRNA and those are able to deliver the RNA to the cells.

VO: Put simply, the synthetic mRNA molecule is squeezed into a tiny oily or waxy sphere.

ITV Professor Arbuthnot [10:57:54:20 - 10:58:29:07] you know, the delivery aspect is not easy to achieve and in fact, I don't think the delivery is quite optimal yet, there’s plenty of room for improvement.

VO: None-the-less, the advances made in the past year have shone a light on how mRNA technology might in future be unleashed on other viruses and diseases. And in sub-Saharan Africa in particular, one virus stands out.
VO: HIV has infected about 76 million people globally. 38 million are living with the virus. More than 30 million have died. Staggering stats; yet, despite several candidates undergoing various levels of testing, a vaccine remains elusive.

ITV Professor Bekker [00:06:16:04 - 00:06:20:00] So this virus is you know, it is stealthy. It truly is extraordinary.

VO: Professor Linda-Gail Bekker is Director of the Desmond Tutu HIV Centre.

ITV Professor Bekker [00:06:16:04 - 00:06:51:08] when we try to design a vaccine, we go for something on the on the surface or some aspect of the pathogen which we know will really stir up our immune systems. (CUT) Now, what HIV does is it disguises those very immunogenic components, it hides it with sugar (CUT) So our immune systems are kind of blind to sugar. And this little pathogen has evolved in such a way that everything that our immune system would get excited about and want to move in and kill that pathogen is covered, if you like, disguised.

VO: HIV has other tricks, too. And it has been aided by a lack of COVID-scale ambition.

ITV Professor Bekker [00:07:54:17 - 00:08:28:07] STRAP Desmond Tutu HIV Centre” we've seen the most amazing galvanizing of resources around Covid. We've never seen that with HIV (CUT) You know, the way the world is just kind of throwing resources at Covid has been eye opening and we've seen terrific results very, very quickly.

VO: In just one example, Moderna received roughly 14 billion Rand in American government grants and a further 23 billion under Operation Warp Speed, a U.S. programme facilitating COVID vaccine development. It’s hoped mRNA’s potential as a platform for the development of other vaccines might level the scales.

ITV Professor Bekker [00:24:29:04 - 00:25:05:03] we've got to reinvigorate the field that it is not OK when a thousand young woman in this country, you know, on a two-weekly basis, become infected with HIV (CUT) we have to see them and engage with them again and then redouble our efforts to say that is not OK in 2021 in South Africa. (CUT) It's policy. It's behaviour, but it's also technology. Right. And I'm quite happy to harness biomedical interventions to help us in this quest (CUT) including vaccines.

VO: For Saidy, it can’t come soon enough.

ITV Saidy Brown [15:08:29:23 - 15:09:02:01] We keep speaking about going towards an HIV free generation (CUT) And I believe that if there was a vaccine for HIV, it would literally, literally change the whole narrative and people would stop viewing HIV or living with HIV and such as a death sentence.

LINK Saidy’s story is a reminder that all we’ve seen and spoken about - the intellectual capital, the high-tech labs, the trials, the successes, the disappointments – is about people trying to find ways to even the odds in a fight that right now, seems utterly one-sided. The “m” in mRNA stands for “messenger” and the message it seems, is one of hope.

ITV Professor Bekker [00:09:33:02 - 00:10:10:07] I've heard through the grapevine (CUT) that there is real movement towards HIV. So particularly the new kids on the block, people who hadn't necessarily, you know, made a lot of products to date. I think they feel perhaps emboldened by their success and, you know, and maybe feeling like this is a feasible goal. So, I'm delighted. The field really needs more players. We need more ideas. I think, you know, we need a vaccine. END>>

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): We examine how the mRNA technology behind several of the COVID vaccines could unlock new ways of fighting other diseases.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Thanks to the extraordinary efforts of leading scientists, the world has been exposed to the wonders of Messenger RNA and its ability to ward off severe COVID19 and, possibly, infection with SARSCoV2. Many, though, are unaware of exactly what mRNA is and how the technology works. We aim to answer those questions while revealing how the success in developing mRNA-based vaccines might lead to new, more effective treatments for other viruses and diseases. It's a case of a unique technology, perfected in unique times, leading to unprecedented advances in modern medicine.
metadata.Summary: Imagine a species so advanced it’s able to replicate the functioning of the human body at a molecular level, one with the audacity to grow in a lab a crucial element of how human cells function and then inject them into actual, living beings. Well, thanks to breakthroughs in Genome sequencing and advances in other areas of medicine, that is precisely what our species is now able to do. It’s a technology at the cutting edge of science and crucial to our attempts to defeat the SARS-CoV-2 virus. However, this is not a Covid story. mRNA is a molecule containing the instructions by which cells make proteins - essential to how our bodies function. What’s the point of proteins? Well, in scientific terms they “are large, complex molecules that play many critical roles in the body. They do most of the work in cells and are required for the structure, function, and regulation of the body’s tissues and organs.” In other words, they’re very important not only to the healthy functioning of our biological systems but to the development of disease and – hopefully – our body’s ability to deal with it. The use of mRNA as the foundational technology in the development of two of the current generation of Covid vaccines (by which our body is “tricked” into making antibodies by recognising a section of the virus’s now infamous spike protein) has confirmed what many have believed for several decades: it's a natural biological process that can be manipulated to help our bodies fight other viruses and diseases. In the southern African context, HIV is one that often comes to mind. So, how does the technology work in lay terms? How did we stumble upon it? Could the darkness of this global pandemic thrust us into the light of a new and infinitely more successful way of treating those suffering currently incurable diseases? And how close might we be to a HIV vaccine, for example?
metadata.Further information: While the development of mRNA-based vaccines has been nothing short of miraculous, those in the know highlight that SARS-CoV-2 is a simpler target than what is presented by other viruses - notably HIV. That's not to say the technology doesn't offer a potentially game-changing approach to how they're treated, merely that much research and study lies ahead to fully unlock its potential.
